Getting Text Ready for NLP

1. The learning map

Computers are good at working with numbers, but a customer review or an email is made of words. Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the area of computing that helps computers work with human language. A typical text project follows this route:

Raw words → cleaned and organized words → a numerical representation → an NLP task. This module introduces the field and focuses on the early preparation steps.

Understand the material

Text is unstructured: documents vary in length, style, and meaning.

Prepare the text

Remove or standardize details that get in the way, then split text into tokens.

Keep the purpose in view

Preprocessing choices can help one task and harm another. There is no universal “clean text” recipe.

2. What is NLP, and why is it challenging?

Natural Language Processing combines ideas from language and computing to help machines analyze or produce human language. The course calls this an applied field because the aim is not only to understand methods, but also to build and assess useful models.

Where text appears in real life

Text is found in social-media posts, web pages, books, product reviews, captions, legal documents, medical records, police reports, and job descriptions. NLP can help with sentiment analysis, classifying documents, plagiarism detection, machine translation, and analyzing the structure of text or code.

Language can be ambiguous

People use context effortlessly; a computer must learn patterns that help resolve it. The same words can have different meanings, and a sentence can be understood in more than one way.

Word-level (lexical) ambiguity

“I went to the bank.” Is it a financial institution or the land beside a river? Nearby words and the situation help us decide.

Sentence-structure (syntactic) ambiguity

“Wafa said on Monday she would give an exam.” Did she speak on Monday, or is the exam on Monday? The sentence structure can allow more than one reading.

Context and missing information

Pronouns such as “it” or “they” depend on what was mentioned earlier. Without context, the intended reference may be unclear.

Memory cue: language ambiguity can live in a word, in the sentence’s structure, or in the surrounding context.

3. Essential NLP vocabulary

TermPlain-language meaningExample
CorpusA collection of text used for reading, analysis, or model building.A folder of customer reviews.
TokenA unit produced when text is split up—often a word, but it could be a punctuation mark or another unit, depending on the tokenizer.“I love tea!” might become I, love, tea, !.
TokenizationSplitting text into tokens.“This is a short sentence” becomes a sequence of words.
VocabularyThe unique tokens recognized in a dataset or by a text representation.If “tea” appears in many reviews, it is still one vocabulary entry.
SyntaxHow words are arranged according to grammar.Word order can change who did what to whom.
Syntactic parsingAnalyzing a sentence’s grammatical structure.Identifying which words belong together in a sentence.
SemanticsThe meaning conveyed by words or text.Understanding that “That’s sick!” may express praise, not illness.
Stop wordA very common word that may contribute little for a particular task.“the,” “a,” “is.” Whether to remove it depends on the goal.
N-gramA sequence of n consecutive tokens.In “a warm cup of tea,” warm cup is a bigram (2-gram).

A unigram contains one token, a bigram two consecutive tokens, and a trigram three. For “this is a simple sentence,” the bigrams include “this is,” “is a,” “a simple,” and “simple sentence.” N-grams can preserve some nearby word combinations that a one-word-at-a-time representation would miss.

4. A practical text-preprocessing pipeline

Text is called unstructured because it does not arrive as a neat, fixed set of numeric columns. Preprocessing prepares it for a task. The lecture introduces three common activities:

  1. Noise removal: handle unwanted formatting such as HTML tags, stray symbols, repeated whitespace, or other irrelevant artifacts.
  2. Tokenization: split a document into the units the method will use.
  3. Normalization: reduce unimportant variation, for example by using consistent letter case or reducing related word forms.

Noise removal

Noise may include HTML markup, accidental control characters, or messy spacing. Depending on the task, punctuation, digits, and accent marks might also be removed or transformed. A regular-expression library (such as Python’s re) can help define text patterns to find and change.

Tokenization

Choose how a document should be divided. Word tokenization is common, but applications may instead split into sentences, subword pieces, or n-grams. For example, a help-desk system might split a message into words first, then create bigrams to retain phrases such as “not working.”

Normalization

Normalization makes selected text forms more consistent. Common examples include lowercasing and reducing related word forms. It can also include removing stop words, rare terms, or task-specific terms—but those decisions should be made with care.

Helpful tools from the lecture: Python’s re module can perform pattern-based cleanup; NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) includes tools for tokenization and word processing.

5. Worked example: sorting customer support messages

Imagine a company wants to find support messages about delivery delays. Here is an illustrative message:

“<p>My order #4821 ISN'T here!!! I ordered two days ago.</p>”
  1. Inspect the goal. We want to find delivery-delay messages. That means “not here,” the order number, and possibly the number of days may all matter.
  2. Clean irrelevant formatting. Remove the HTML paragraph tags and normalize repeated spaces. Keep the message itself.
  3. Choose case handling. Lowercase words so “ISN'T” and “isn't” are treated alike. But preserve or correctly normalize the negation.
  4. Tokenize. One possible result is my, order, 4821, isn't, here, i, ordered, two, days, ago.
  5. Consider normalization. A lemmatizer might map ordered to order; however, the original message may also refer to an order, so the surrounding phrase remains useful.
  6. Build useful features. A bigram such as not here (if tokenization separates the contraction in a suitable way) can capture a clue that separate words alone may obscure.
Important: removing “not” as a stop word could turn “not delivered” into “delivered,” reversing the meaning. Removing all digits could also discard an order number that is useful for customer service. These examples are illustrative; the right preprocessing depends on what the system needs to do.

6. Stemming, lemmatization, and careful choices

MethodWhat it doesSimple illustration
StemmingUses rules that often chop prefixes or suffixes to produce a shorter stem. The result need not be a dictionary word.“connected,” “connecting,” and “connection” may be reduced to a shared stem-like form by a particular stemmer; exact output depends on the rules.
LemmatizationUses lexical or linguistic knowledge to map a word to a recognized base form (lemma).“was” may map to “be”; “better” may map to “good” when the tool has the needed context.

Both can reduce variation, but lemmatization aims for a linguistically valid base form instead of simply trimming word endings. A lemmatizer may need part-of-speech or context information to choose correctly.

Preprocessing is a choice, not a checklist

Removing punctuation, numbers, accents, or common words can be useful in some tasks and harmful in others. Punctuation can express excitement or distinguish a question. Numbers may be prices, dates, or order IDs. Stop words such as “not” can reverse meaning. Text models trained with embeddings may rely on word context, so aggressive cleanup can remove clues the model needs.

Ask: what is noise here?

For topic discovery, an order ID may be clutter. For customer support, it may be essential.

Ask: what distinction matters?

Lowercasing may help match “Tea” with “tea,” but case may matter for names or acronyms.

Check the result

Compare performance on examples the model did not learn from. Do not assume more cleaning always means a better model.

Memory cue: clean what is irrelevant, split into useful pieces, and standardize only the differences that do not matter to the task.

8. Self-check

1. What is a corpus?

A collection of text. A set of customer reviews or a collection of news articles can each be a corpus.

2. What is the difference between syntax and semantics?

Syntax is the grammatical structure or arrangement of words. Semantics is the meaning conveyed by the text.

3. What is a bigram?

A sequence of two consecutive tokens, such as “very helpful” in the text “very helpful staff.”

4. How do stemming and lemmatization differ?

Stemming often chops word endings using rules and may produce a non-word stem. Lemmatization uses linguistic or lexical knowledge to seek a valid base form.

5. Why should you not automatically remove every number or stop word?

Some numbers carry useful information, such as a price or order ID, and some common words carry meaning, especially “not.” The task determines what is useful.

6. A customer writes “I am not happy.” Why could deleting “not” be dangerous?

It reverses the sentiment clue: “not happy” and “happy” do not mean the same thing.

Quick recall: NLP works with human language; preprocessing cleans and organizes text for a task; always preserve the words and details that carry the meaning your task needs.
